questions.question: How does term-at-a-time scoring traverse an inverted index?
options: It finishes one candidate document before opening the next posting list
It scans documents in stored file order and rescores each one in place
It consumes one query term's postings fully before starting the next
It visits only the documents already sitting in the top-k result heap

questions.question: What state does a basic term-at-a-time scorer use to combine contributions?
options: A dictionary of phrases ordered by their position in the document
An accumulator keyed by document identifier, holding partial sums
A min-heap holding one entry for every term in the vocabulary
A table of stored query norms, one row per term in the query

questions.question: What is a key memory advantage of document-at-a-time top-k scoring?
options: Each score is final at once, so only a size-k heap is retained
A dense score array is kept for the whole collection at every step
Posting iterators are discarded, leaving only the term upper bounds
Document identifiers are no longer needed once traversal has begun

questions.question: In conjunctive document-at-a-time retrieval, which iterator movement is useful?
options: Rewinding every list to its first posting after each match is found
Advancing the longest posting list forward by exactly one entry
Decoding term positions before any document identifier is compared
Seeking every lagging list forward to the largest current identifier

questions.question: Postings are a:(2,1.5),(5,0.7) and b:(2,0.8),(7,1.2). What score is finalized for document 2 under additive scoring?
Why should an optimized traversal be compared with an exhaustive reference scorer?
options: To confirm that compression has reduced the size of the stored postings
To force every query in production onto the term-at-a-time path
To prove the faster traversal returns the same ranking as before
To replace relevance judgments with a purely mechanical measurement

questions.question: What does a champion list normally contain for a term?
options: The documents whose identifiers are smallest within that term's posting
The r documents carrying the largest term-specific weights for it
The documents that were most recently added and contain that term
The queries that have previously included the term in production

questions.question: What is the primary goal of index elimination?
options: To grow the indexed vocabulary so more query terms find postings
To keep word order inside each posting so phrases can be matched
To score every candidate twice so that ties can be broken safely
To cut the postings or candidates that ranking has to consider

questions.question: What happens when champion-list size r is made smaller?
options: Candidate cost usually falls while the risk of a miss rises
Candidate cost and the risk of a miss both fall together
Exhaustive top-k results become guaranteed at every budget
Term-specific weights stop deciding which documents enter

questions.question: Why can a document outside every per-term champion list still be highly relevant?
options: Champion lists are built only from documents already deleted
A document outside the lists must contain none of the query terms
Moderate evidence on several terms can sum to a strong total
A document identifier changes the weighting formula that applies

questions.question: A first tier returns k documents at threshold 0.15, while an omitted candidate may score 0.9. What should the ranker do?
options: Stop, because the heap already holds the k results requested
Return the single strongest first-tier document and no others
Set every omitted candidate's score to zero and finish the query
Search the fallback tier, because stopping cannot yet be justified

questions.question: Which evaluation most directly quantifies champion-list quality?
options: The mean spelling length of the terms held in the vocabulary
Recall of the exhaustive top k at a fixed candidate budget
The count of index segments searched during a typical query
The share of query terms dropped before traversal begins

questions.question: What information lets WAND skip candidates safely?
options: Valid upper bounds on what each query term can contribute
A random sample of the document identifiers in each posting
The number of postings remaining in each of the query's lists
A fixed champion-list size shared by all of the query terms

questions.question: What is the top-k threshold after a min-heap of k competitive results is full?
options: The largest score currently sitting in the heap
The sum of the upper bounds of all query terms
The smallest score currently held in the heap
The score of the most recently indexed document

questions.question: Upper bounds 0.4, 0.7, and 0.8 are accumulated against threshold 1.5. At which cumulative value can the WAND pivot be selected?
Why does pruning usually strengthen after good results have been found?
options: The posting lists lose their document-identifier ordering
The upper bound stored for each term turns negative
The query acquires additional terms as scoring proceeds
The heap threshold rises, so more candidates fail it

questions.question: What is the correctness consequence of underestimating a term upper bound?
options: More harmless candidates than necessary are fully scored
A genuine top-k document can be skipped entirely
The top-k heap grows beyond the k entries requested
Every candidate document receives an identical score

questions.question: Why can block-level maximum scores outperform one global maximum per term?
options: They give tighter local bounds, so many more blocks can be skipped
They remove the bound metadata that a posting list must store
They leave the postings unsorted, which speeds up decoding
They cause filters to accept every candidate that is generated
